units.title: Model-free prediction and first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo
outcomes: Derive first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo return averages for a fixed policy from sampled episodes.
Implement first-visit Monte Carlo prediction from a blank file and match exact return averages on fixed episodes.
Explain why first-visit averages are unbiased through the law of large numbers and why every-visit averages need more care.
units.why: Without a transition model, complete episode returns are the only exact target available. Monte Carlo turns those returns into value estimates and sets the baseline every TD method is compared against.

next.note: Carry the averaging update into its incremental form.
Compare full-return targets with one-step bootstrapped targets.

study.title: DP, MC and TD as three ways to edit one table
study.locator: Section Monte Carlo with the corridor trajectory and the every-visit update table (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read as a worked comparison, not as the update contract. Keep the Sutton box as the contract.

focus: Model-free means no \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) or \(R(s, a)\) table is used. The target \(G_t\) comes from a sampled episode, with \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \cdots\).

First-visit averages the return after the first visit to \(s\) in each episode. Every-visit averages all visits. The boxed algorithm implements first-visit; every-visit drops the earlier-occurrence check.
Monte Carlo waits for termination, so it applies to episodic tasks only. No update happens step by step.
Each first-visit return is an independent unbiased sample of \(v_{\pi}(s)\), so the average converges by the law of large numbers with standard deviation falling as \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement first-visit Monte Carlo prediction and run it on `[[(0, 1.0), (1, 1.0), (2, 1.0)]]` with `gamma=1.0` to get `[3.0, 2.0, 1.0]`, then on `[[(0, 1.0), (1, 1.0), (0, 1.0), (2, 0.0)]]` to get `[3.0, 2.0, 0.0]`. State which visit each return belongs to.
traps: Averaging all visits while calling the result first-visit. A repeated state in one episode contributes once under first-visit and every time under every-visit.
Updating before the episode ends. The return \(G_t\) is not known until termination, so an intermediate average uses an incomplete sum.
Reading the blackjack figure as exact values. Figure 5.1 after 500,000 games is a close approximation, and usable-ace states stay noisier because they are visited less often.

selfTest.q: Why does Monte Carlo prediction require episodic tasks?
selfTest.a: Its target is the complete return, which is only known at termination. Without a terminal step there is no \(G_t\) to average.

selfTest.q: One episode yields state rewards 1, 1, 1, 0 across visits to states 0, 1, 0, 2. What does each method record for state 0?
selfTest.a: First-visit records one return, 3. Every-visit records two returns, 3 and 1.

selfTest.q: Why is the first-visit average unbiased for \(v_{\pi}(s)\)?
selfTest.a: Each first-visit return is an independent sample of \(v_{\pi}(s)\) with finite variance, so its expectation equals \(v_{\pi}(s)\) and the average converges to it.

selfTest.q: How do the error bars shrink with more first visits?
selfTest.a: The standard deviation of the average falls as \(1/\sqrt{n}\) with \(n\) first visits.

units.title: Incremental means, constant step sizes and learning-rate conditions
outcomes: Derive the incremental mean update and the constant step-size update from the averaging definition.
State the step-size convergence conditions and explain which part tracking violates and why.
Predict how initialization bias decays under decreasing versus constant step sizes.
units.why: Every tabular update in this section is an incremental average in disguise. The step-size choice decides whether old bias dies out or new samples keep overwriting the past.

next.note: Use the same update template with a bootstrapped target.
Connect visit counts to effective step sizes.

study.title: Incremental and tracking updates
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.4 and 2.5, equations (2.3) to (2.7) with Exercises 2.4 and 2.5 (printed pp. 30 to 33)
study.depth: Skip the bandit testbed and action-selection sections; read only the update rules and the step-size discussion.

study.title: Constant step-size arithmetic in the corridor tables
study.locator: The MC and TD worked tables, which both move old values toward targets with \(\alpha = 0.5\) (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the tables as arithmetic examples of constant step sizes, not as converged values.

focus: The general template is \(Q_{n+1} = Q_n + \alpha_n(R_n - Q_n)\) from (2.4). The sample mean uses \(\alpha_n = 1/n\); tracking uses constant \(\alpha\) from (2.5).
Constant \(\alpha\) gives recent rewards exponentially more weight, \((1 - \alpha)^{n-i}\), so the initial bias decays but old samples are discounted forever.
Convergence needs \(\sum_n \alpha_n = \infty\) with \(\sum_n \alpha_n^2 < \infty\) from (2.7). Constant \(\alpha\) fails the second sum, which is why it tracks drift instead of converging.
Visitation gates learning: rarely visited pairs take fewer steps, so their estimates move slower at any shared \(\alpha\).
units.reproduce: Starting from \(Q_1 = 0\) with rewards \(1, 2, 3\) in order and \(\alpha = 0.5\), apply \(Q_{n+1} = Q_n + \alpha(R_n - Q_n)\) three times and get \(Q_4 = 2.125\). Expand the weights as in (2.6) and show the weight on \(R_3\) is \(0.5\) while the weight on \(R_1\) is \(0.125\). Confirm the decreasing step-size mean gives exactly \(2\).
traps: Using \(\alpha = 1\) everywhere because it removes bias fastest. It also removes all memory, so one noisy reward decides the estimate.
Assuming constant \(\alpha\) converges because early bias decays. The bias from \(Q_1\) decays as \((1 - \alpha)^n\), but the variance never settles since every new sample keeps weight \(\alpha\).
Treating unvisited pairs as learned. No visit means no update at that step size; a shared schedule does not teach pairs the behavior policy never tries.

selfTest.q: Rewards arrive as 10 then 0 with \(Q_1 = 0\) and constant \(\alpha = 0.5\). What is \(Q_3\)?
selfTest.a: \(Q_2 = 5\), then \(Q_3 = 5 + 0.5(0 - 5) = 2.5\). The first reward keeps weight \(0.25\).

selfTest.q: Which convergence sum does constant \(\alpha\) violate?
selfTest.a: The squares sum: \(\sum_n \alpha^2\) diverges for constant \(\alpha\), so noise never averages out. The plain sum \(\sum_n \alpha_n = \infty\) still holds.

selfTest.q: Why does \(\alpha_n = 1/n\) converge slowly in practice?
selfTest.a: Later samples get weight \(1/n\), so after many visits each new return barely moves the estimate even when the policy has changed.

selfTest.q: A pair is visited once in 10,000 steps. What does a shared step size imply?
selfTest.a: Its estimate took one step from initialization. Visit counts gate learning; the schedule cannot compensate for missing coverage.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: constant versus decreasing step-size comparisons with matched interaction budgets and visitation logs.
units.stopWhen: You derive (2.4) to (2.7) closed-book, reproduce the 2.125 weighting by hand, and can predict which schedule tracks a drift and which converges.

fit.note: Sections 2.4 and 2.5 with equations (2.3) to (2.7) cover both topics at derive depth; step-size practice runs inside the mini-project comparison.

units.title: TD error, TD(0), bootstrapping and Monte Carlo versus TD bias and variance
outcomes: Derive the TD(0) update and the TD error from the Bellman expectation equation.

Compare Monte Carlo and TD(0) on sample efficiency and bias using the random-walk evidence.
units.why: TD learns from every step instead of every episode. That single change buys sample efficiency at the price of bootstrapping bias, and the rest of the section reuses the same error.

Lift TD(0) prediction into action-value control.

study.depth: Use the lecture's TD update framing; leave Q-learning to Lecture 4.

study.title: Online TD updates on one trajectory
study.locator: Section Temporal Difference with the step-by-step corridor table that reuses updated values mid-episode (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Treat the corridor numbers as one sampled trajectory, not as converged values.

focus: The TD error \(\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)\) from (6.5) is the gap between the one-step target and the old estimate. TD(0) from (6.2) moves \(V(S_t)\) by \(\alpha \delta_t\).
TD(0) replaces the unknown tail \(G_{t+1}\) with the current estimate \(V(S_{t+1})\). That substitution is bootstrapping: an estimate updates another estimate.

Monte Carlo is unbiased with high variance and waits for termination. TD(0) has lower variance, learns online each step, but is biased until the successor estimates are accurate. Example 6.2 finds TD consistently ahead of constant-\(\alpha\) Monte Carlo on RMS error for the step sizes it tries; Exercise 6.4 asks whether a wider range would change that.
The corridor TD table reads already-updated cells mid-episode, so later steps build on earlier corrections. That reuse is the online mechanism, not a bookkeeping error.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute the TD error for \(V(s) = 5\), \(R_{t+1} = 1\), \(V(S_{t+1}) = 10\) and \(\gamma = 0.9\) with no termination to get \(\delta_t = 5\), and for \(V(s) = 8\), \(R_{t+1} = 10\) at termination to get \(\delta_t = 2\). Then update \(V(s) = 5\) with \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(\delta_t = 5\) to get \(5.5\).
traps: Calling TD(0) unbiased because it uses a real reward. The reward is real but \(V(S_{t+1})\) is an estimate, so the target inherits its error.
Zeroing the bootstrap on any episode end. Termination sets the beyond-end value to zero; truncation must keep bootstrapping. The alignment unit makes this exact.
Comparing single-seed learning curves as proof. Example 6.2 averages many runs; one seed can favor either method.

selfTest.q: What are the Monte Carlo and TD(0) targets for the same transition?
selfTest.a: Monte Carlo uses the full sampled return \(G_t\). TD(0) uses \(R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})\).

selfTest.q: Why does TD(0) learn before termination?
selfTest.a: Its target needs only one reward and the next state's current estimate, so it updates each step instead of waiting for \(G_t\).

selfTest.q: A learner zeroes the bootstrap at a time limit. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The value loses the future return beyond the limit. Time limits truncate; only true termination zeroes the bootstrap.

selfTest.q: When does TD(0) beat Monte Carlo on the random walk?
selfTest.a: In Example 6.2, TD(0) stays below constant-\(\alpha\) Monte Carlo on RMS error over the first 100 episodes for every step size shown. The ranking depends on step sizes, so compare each method at its best \(\alpha\).

units.title: n-step returns, target boundaries and fixed-trajectory update oracles
outcomes: Derive n-step returns with their TD, Sarsa and off-policy update forms for a fixed trajectory.
State the target boundary rule: zero-pad at termination and bootstrap only inside the trajectory.
Implement fixed-trajectory update oracles that match hand-computed n-step targets exactly.
units.why: One-step and full-episode targets are two ends of one spectrum. n-step returns fill the middle, and fixed-trajectory oracles make every later update testable without running an agent.

next.note: See which n-step updates need behavior-policy corrections.

study.title: n-step TD, n-step Sarsa and n-step off-policy updates
study.locator: Chapter 7, Sections 7.1 to 7.3, equations (7.1) to (7.5) with Figures 7.1 to 7.3, ending before starred Section 7.4 (printed pp. 142 to 150)
study.depth: Stop before starred Section 7.4. Eligibility traces stay out; this unit ends at n-step oracles.

study.title: Fixed-trajectory checks in the control laboratory
study.locator: Milestone A and Correctness requirements: exact and fixed-trajectory update checks
study.depth: Read for what an oracle must check, not for DQN or policy-gradient material.

focus: The n-step return \(G_{t:t+n} = R_{t+1} + \cdots + \gamma^{n-1}R_{t+n} + \gamma^n V_{t+n-1}(S_{t+n})\) sums \(n\) real rewards then bootstraps. At \(n = 1\) it is TD(0); as \(n\) grows it approaches Monte Carlo.
If \(t + n\) reaches termination, missing terms are zero and no bootstrap is added. The boundary sits at \(T\), not at a fixed \(n\).
The error-reduction bound (7.3) says the worst-case error contracts by \(\gamma^n\): longer \(n\) trusts the current \(V\) less.
An oracle takes an explicit trajectory and returns the exact target. It never steps an environment, so failures in it are update bugs, not sampling noise.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, take one episode of single-reward steps from zero values with `gamma=0.9` and `alpha=0.1`. Show `n=1` gives `[0.1, 0.1, 0.1]` and `n=2` gives `[0.19, 0.19, 0.1]`, with the `n=2` target at the first state equal to `1.9`.
traps: Shifting the reward index by one. \(R_{t+1}\) follows \(S_t\); pairing \(R_t\) with \(S_t\) corrupts every n-step sum.
Bootstrapping past termination. Once the episode ends at \(T\), the target is the zero-padded sum, never plus \(\gamma^n V\).
Testing updates through a live agent. Environment noise then masks off-by-one errors that a fixed trajectory would expose exactly.

selfTest.q: Write \(G_{t:t+2}\) in full.
selfTest.a: \(G_{t:t+2} = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 V(S_{t+2})\), or the zero-padded sum when the episode ends first.

selfTest.q: Why can no real algorithm use \(G_{t:t+n}\) at time \(t+1\)?
selfTest.a: It needs rewards and states up to \(t+n\), which have not happened yet. The update for \(S_t\) waits until time \(t+n\).

selfTest.q: What does (7.3) promise when the current values are already exact?
selfTest.a: Nothing beyond exactness: if the worst error is zero, the n-step expectation is exact for every \(n\).

selfTest.q: An oracle and a live run disagree. Which do you trust?
selfTest.a: The oracle, after checking its hand computation. It removes sampling noise, so a mismatch points at the live update or its boundary handling.

study.depth: Compare what each box learns versus what generates its data; leave Expected Sarsa and maximization bias to later units.

study.title: On-policy versus off-policy framing
study.locator: Lecture 4, On and Off-Policy Learning (slide 34), with Q-learning as the off-policy case (slide 35)
study.depth: Use the framing only; the derivations live in Sutton.

focus: The behavior policy \(b\) generates actions. The target policy \(\pi\) is the one being evaluated or improved. On-policy means \(b = \pi\); off-policy means they differ.

Sarsa backs up \(Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})\) with the action actually taken, so it evaluates the behavior policy. Q-learning backs up \(\max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a)\) regardless of the next action, so it directly approximates \(q_*\).
Coverage requires \(\pi(a \mid s) > 0\) to imply \(b(a \mid s) > 0\). Without it some target actions never appear and no weight can repair the gap.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, classify Sarsa, Q-learning and Expected Sarsa as on-policy or off-policy under behavior policy \(b\), and write the coverage condition. Then give a two-action case where \(\pi\) picks the unsupported action and state the conclusion: nothing about that action.
traps: Calling Q-learning on-policy because one policy object acts and updates. The target uses the max, not the behavior action, so the learned values are off-policy even with a single actor.
Assuming greedy behavior is safe for Sarsa. Without exploration Sarsa stops updating unvisited pairs and can lock onto a suboptimal policy.
Believing more off-policy data always helps. Data from \(b\) without coverage of \(\pi\) adds no information about the missing actions.

selfTest.q: Why is Q-learning off-policy even when actions come from its own \(\epsilon\)-greedy policy?
selfTest.a: Its target uses the maximum over next actions, not the action the behavior policy will take. It learns about the greedy policy while behaving \(\epsilon\)-greedy.

selfTest.q: Suppose action selection is fully greedy with identical initialization and tie-breaking. Do Sarsa and Q-learning behave identically?
selfTest.a: Almost, but not exactly. Sarsa picks \(A_{t+1}\) before updating \(Q(S_t, A_t)\), while Q-learning picks its next action after the update, so when \(S_{t+1} = S_t\) the update can change which action is greedy and the two runs diverge. Exercise 6.12 asks exactly this.

selfTest.q: Behavior never tries action up in some state. What can off-policy learning say about it?
selfTest.a: Nothing. Coverage fails, so no trajectory carries information about that pair.

selfTest.q: Which policy's values does on-policy Monte Carlo control improve?
selfTest.a: The \(\epsilon\)-soft behavior policy it samples from, per Section 5.4. Optimality comes only as exploration decays.

units.title: Trajectory and per-decision importance sampling, ordinary and weighted estimators
outcomes: Derive trajectory importance ratios and the per-decision form that drops irrelevant future factors.
Implement ordinary and weighted importance-sampling estimators on fixed trajectories.
Explain why ordinary sampling is unbiased with high variance while weighted sampling trades bias for lower variance.
units.why: Off-policy data has the wrong action probabilities. Importance ratios reweight it back, and the choice of estimator decides whether variance or bias dominates.

next.note: Diagnose when the weights collapse.
Revisit these estimators for off-policy evaluation.

study.title: Off-policy prediction via importance sampling
study.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.5, equations (5.3) to (5.6) with Examples 5.4 and 5.5 and Figures 5.3 and 5.4 (printed pp. 103 to 109)
study.depth: Read the ordinary-versus-weighted comparison closely; leave incremental implementation to Section 5.6.

study.title: Per-decision importance sampling
study.locator: Starred Section 5.9 on per-decision importance sampling, equations (5.11) to (5.14) (printed pp. 114 to 115)
study.depth: Read only the per-decision expectation argument; skip discounting-aware Section 5.8 unless the discounted case needs it.

focus: The trajectory ratio \(\rho_{t:T-1} = \prod_{k=t}^{T-1} \frac{\pi(A_k \mid S_k)}{b(A_k \mid S_k)}\) corrects the whole-trajectory probability. Its expectation under \(b\) is \(1\).
Ordinary sampling averages \(\rho G\) and is unbiased. Weighted sampling divides by the summed ratios; it is biased but its variance stays controlled and no single return takes weight above \(1\).
Per-decision sampling scales each reward \(R_{t+k}\) only by ratios up to \(t+k-1\). Later factors have expectation \(1\) given the reward, so dropping them keeps the expectation and cuts variance.
Example 5.5 shows ordinary sampling failing to settle after millions of episodes on a looping MDP while weighted sampling converges. Long products are the mechanism.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, take two trajectories with returns \(G = 2\) and \(G = 0\) and ratios \(\rho = 2\) and \(\rho = 0.5\). Compute the ordinary estimate as \((2 \times 2 + 0.5 \times 0)/2 = 2\) and the weighted estimate as \(4/2.5 = 1.6\).
traps: Multiplying ratios past the reward they correct. The per-decision argument shows those factors add variance with no change in expectation.
Normalizing the weighted estimator by the episode count instead of the summed weights. Equation (5.6) divides by the weight sum; dividing by \(n\) rebuilds the ordinary estimator's scale.
Trusting ordinary sampling on looping trajectories. Example 5.5 is the warning: a few huge ratios dominate the average.

selfTest.q: What is \(\rho_{t:T-1}\) when \(\pi = b\)?
selfTest.a: Every factor is 1, so the product is 1 and both estimators reduce to plain Monte Carlo.

selfTest.q: Why does weighted sampling have lower variance than ordinary sampling?
selfTest.a: It divides by the observed weight sum, so the largest weight on any return is 1. Ordinary sampling lets rare huge ratios scale returns without bound.

selfTest.q: A reward at \(t+1\) is scaled by ratios up to \(T-1\). Which factors can go?
selfTest.a: All factors after \(t\). Their conditional expectation is \(1\), so per-decision estimation drops them.

selfTest.q: The behavior policy never takes an action the target takes. What happens to the ratio?
selfTest.a: It divides by zero. Coverage fails before any estimator runs; see the previous unit.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: ordinary and weighted estimates on fixed trajectories with a coverage-failure case.

study.locator: Env `step` returning `terminated` and `truncated` with `info`, and `reset` with `seed`: log `observation`, `action`, `reward`, `terminated` and `truncated` each step (Gymnasium 1.4.0; page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Visitation instrumentation in the control laboratory
study.locator: Milestone B and Measurement requirements: visitation records with per-seed raw curves

focus: Support means \(b(a \mid s) > 0\) wherever \(\pi(a \mid s) > 0\). Effective sample size \(\text{ESS} = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2\) drops toward \(1\) when one weight dominates and equals \(n\) for equal weights.
Visitation counts come from logged trajectories, not from \(Q\) magnitudes. A large \(Q\) on an unvisited pair is initialization, not knowledge.
Coverage is a property of the data-collection policy and the logging code. Changing the estimator cannot create visits that never happened.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, take weights `[2.0, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0]` and compute \(\text{ESS} = 16/5.5 \approx 2.91\) against \(n = 4\), then flag a state-action pair with zero visits as uncovered in a small visitation table.
traps: Reporting raw episode counts as coverage. Ten thousand episodes that avoid a pair still leave it uncovered.
Averaging effective sample size across mismatched policies. Weights from different \(b\) versions are not one sample; version the behavior policy first.
Reading \(\text{ESS} = n\) as success. Equal weights with tiny \(n\) still leave large standard errors.

selfTest.q: Weights are all equal. What is the effective sample size?
selfTest.a: \(\text{ESS} = n\). Each sample carries full weight.

selfTest.q: One weight is 100 and ninety-nine are near zero. What does the size say?
selfTest.a: About 1. The average is effectively one trajectory.

selfTest.q: A pair has zero visits but a high \(Q\). What do you report?
selfTest.a: Uncovered. The value is initialization, not evidence.

selfTest.q: Can weighted sampling fix zero support?
selfTest.a: No. Its ratio needs \(b > 0\); missing support means the estimand is unidentified from this data.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: visitation logs, effective-sample-size curves and a planted coverage-failure case.
units.stopWhen: You compute effective sample size on a weight vector without notes, produce a visitation table that names uncovered pairs, and refuse an estimate with missing support.

fit.note: Sections 5.5 and 5.7 supply support and variance, Gymnasium supplies the loggable step fields, and the laboratory supplies visitation practice through the mini-project.

units.title: SARSA and Expected SARSA control
outcomes: Derive the Sarsa and Expected Sarsa targets and state which policy each evaluates.
Implement both updates from a blank file and match fixed-trajectory values exactly.
Explain when Expected Sarsa reduces variance relative to Sarsa and when it matches Q-learning.
units.why: These are the two on-policy TD control updates. They turn evaluation into improvement while staying on the behavior policy's data.

next.note: Contrast with the off-policy max target.
See the risky-path split under exploration.

study.title: Sarsa and Expected Sarsa
study.locator: Chapter 6, Sections 6.4 and 6.6, rules (6.7) and (6.9) with the Sarsa box and equation (6.9) (printed pp. 129 to 133)
study.depth: Skip Section 6.5 Q-learning and Section 6.7 maximization bias here.

study.title: On-policy TD control
study.locator: Lecture 4, Model-free Policy Iteration with TD Methods (slide 33) and the SARSA update under Properties of TD-Style Tabular Control (slide 38)
study.depth: Use the lecture's control framing; the update contracts live in Sutton.

focus: Sarsa's target \(R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})\) uses the action actually taken next. It evaluates the behavior policy, including its exploration.
Expected Sarsa replaces the sampled \(Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})\) with \(\sum_a \pi(a \mid S_{t+1}) Q(S_{t+1}, a)\). Same expectation, less variance from random next actions.
With a greedy target policy the expectation becomes the max, so Expected Sarsa matches the Q-learning target while keeping the Sarsa update schema.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, load `Q = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]` and process the transition `(0, 0, 1.0, 1, False)` with `alpha=0.1`, `gamma=0.9` and `epsilon=0.1`. Show the expected next value is \(0.05 \times 3.0 + 0.95 \times 4.0 = 3.95\) and the updated value is \(Q(0, 0) = 1.3555\).
traps: Using the max in the Sarsa target. That turns it into Q-learning and silently changes the evaluated policy.
Computing the expectation under \(b\) instead of \(\pi\). Expected Sarsa averages with target-policy probabilities.
Forgetting the terminal mask in Expected Sarsa. At termination the expectation term drops out just like any bootstrap.

selfTest.q: Write both targets.
selfTest.a: Sarsa: \(R_{t+1} + \gamma Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})\). Expected Sarsa: \(R_{t+1} + \gamma \sum_a \pi(a \mid S_{t+1}) Q(S_{t+1}, a)\).

selfTest.q: Why does Expected Sarsa have lower variance than Sarsa at fixed \(\alpha\)?
selfTest.a: It averages over next-action randomness analytically instead of sampling one \(A_{t+1}\).

selfTest.q: Behavior turns fully greedy with a greedy target. What happens to the three targets?
selfTest.a: Expected Sarsa's target becomes the Q-learning max exactly. Sarsa's sampled next action is greedy too, but it is chosen before the update, so when \(S_{t+1} = S_t\) the update can change the greedy action and Sarsa can still differ from Q-learning (Exercise 6.12).

selfTest.q: A learner updates \(Q(S_t, A_t)\) with the action from two steps later. What broke?
selfTest.a: Action alignment. The target must use the action at \(t+1\), not a later one; stale next actions bias control.

units.title: Q-learning and \(\epsilon\)-greedy exploration schedules
outcomes: Implement Q-learning with \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior and match fixed updates exactly.
Derive \(\epsilon\)-greedy action probabilities and design a decay schedule that keeps visiting all pairs.
Explain why Q-learning converges toward optimal values while its behavior stays exploratory.
units.why: Q-learning learns optimal values from exploratory data. The max target separates what is learned from how data is collected, and \(\epsilon\) schedules decide whether every pair gets visited.

next.note: Test the max target on the cliff.
Carry \(\epsilon\) schedules into deep exploration.

study.title: Q-learning and \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior
study.locator: Chapter 6, Sections 6.4 and 6.5, rule (6.8) with the Q-learning box (printed pp. 129 to 132)
study.depth: Focus on the max target and \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior; leave Expected Sarsa to the previous unit.

study.title: Q-learning convergence and coverage
study.locator: Lecture 4, \(\epsilon\)-greedy policies and their improvement (slides 19 to 21), GLIE (slides 29 to 30), Q-learning with \(\epsilon\)-greedy exploration (slides 35 to 36) and Convergence Properties of Q-Learning with the Robbins-Monro step-size conditions (slide 37)
study.depth: Use the assumption statements; the function-approximation half of the lecture belongs to the next section.

study.title: \(\epsilon\)-greedy as a seed-sensitive choice
study.locator: Section 2.1 on exploration and exploitation with the bandit comparison (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the method ranking as seed-dependent and compare across seeds; one run proves nothing.

focus: Q-learning's target \(R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a)\) assumes the greedy action next, whatever \(A_{t+1}\) was. Convergence needs all pairs visited repeatedly plus standard step-size conditions.

\(\epsilon\)-greedy picks the greedy action with probability \(1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/|\mathcal{A}|\) and each other action with \(\epsilon/|\mathcal{A}|\). With \(\epsilon = 0.1\) and two actions that is \(0.95\) and \(0.05\).
Decay \(\epsilon\) toward zero for asymptotic optimality, but keep it high enough early that coverage precedes exploitation. The cliff unit shows what happens otherwise.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, process a single-action chain ending at a terminal state with rewards `1.0`, `2.0` and `3.0` using `alpha=0.5` and `gamma=0.9` from zero values to get `Q('A', 'go') = 0.5000`, `Q('B', 'go') = 1.0000` and `Q('C', 'go') = 1.5000`. State why the max changes nothing on this chain.
traps: Decaying \(\epsilon\) to zero before values settle. Behavior turns greedy around bad values and coverage ends early.
Copying action indices across libraries. Deep-ML 518 orders the four moves up, down, left, right while Gymnasium orders them up, right, down, left. Index by name, not by number.
Reading online return as the learned policy's value. Under \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior, online returns include exploration steps; evaluate the greedy policy separately.

selfTest.q: With \(\epsilon = 0.2\) and four actions, what is the greedy-action probability?
Why can Q-learning learn \(q_*\) from random behavior?
selfTest.a: Its target bootstraps the max, so updates point at the optimal values whenever all pairs keep being visited, regardless of which policy visits them.

selfTest.q: Greedy actions tie. How should ties break?
selfTest.a: Deterministically and documented, for example lowest index. Deep-ML relies on `np.argmax` returning index 0.

selfTest.q: Online average improves while the greedy policy is unchanged. What happened?
selfTest.a: Exploration artifacts or luck. Report the greedy policy's return on separate evaluation seeds.

practice.name: Deep-ML 133: Q-Learning

units.title: SARSA versus Q-learning on risky paths, with multiple seeds and independent evaluation
outcomes: Explain why Sarsa learns the safe path and Q-learning learns the cliff edge under shared \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior.
Run a multi-seed cliff comparison with independent evaluation streams and report spread, not one run.
Attribute the performance gap to update-distribution effects, not to tuning.
units.why: This is the on-policy versus off-policy split made visible. Identical exploration produces different policies because each update prices risk differently.

next.note: Check the cliff bootstrap handles falls correctly.
Reuse the multi-seed discipline on sparse rewards.

study.title: Cliff walking: on-policy versus off-policy under risk
study.locator: Chapter 6, Example 6.6 with its episode-reward graph (printed pp. 131 to 133)
study.depth: Read the online-performance explanation closely: Q-learning learns optimal values but falls in more often during training.

study.title: CliffWalking environment contract
study.locator: Environment description: start state, goal state, cliff penalty with return to start, and the four-action movement set (Gymnasium 1.4.0; page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the installed release behavior you check by running it; the page text is the contract, not the dynamics proof.

study.title: Matched budgets for the comparison
study.locator: Measurement requirements: matched interaction budgets with per-seed raw curves

focus: Sarsa prices the exploration it actually does: its updates include the \(\epsilon\)-greedy falls, so the safe path wins. Q-learning prices the max, so the cliff edge wins on values while behavior still falls.
Online episode return mixes learning and exploration. Compare greedy-policy evaluation streams on held-out seeds, averaged over many runs as in Figure 6.3.
Use the same \(\epsilon\), the same \(\alpha\) and the same seeds for both algorithms. Otherwise the gap may come from tuning, not from the update.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, build the 4 by 12 cliff grid with start `(3, 0)`, goal `(3, 11)`, cliff cells `(3, 1)` to `(3, 10)`, reward `-1` per step and `-100` on cliff entry with return to start. Verify single transitions: stepping into the cliff returns the start with `-100`, and reaching the goal ends the episode.
traps: Judging by learned values alone. The Q-learning values sit closer to optimal while its online return is worse; report both.
Running one seed each. Cliff falls are rare events; single runs move the averages by ten points or more. Keep every seed.
Correcting the Gymnasium page number for Example 6.6. Its page 132 matches the second-edition printed page; cite the example number anyway, since printings and PDF page counts differ.

selfTest.q: Both algorithms use identical \(\epsilon\)-greedy behavior. Why do their paths differ?
selfTest.a: Their targets differ. Sarsa backs up the exploratory action including falls; Q-learning backs up the max, which ignores the fall risk during learning.

selfTest.q: The Q-learning sum of rewards per episode is worse although its values are more optimal. Explain.
selfTest.a: Online returns count exploration falls. The values describe the greedy policy; the behavior policy keeps stepping off the edge.

selfTest.q: What happens as \(\epsilon\) decays to zero for both?
selfTest.a: Both converge toward the optimal policy. The book states this at the end of Example 6.6.

selfTest.q: A comparison tunes \(\epsilon\) separately per algorithm and declares a winner. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: The tuning budget differs, so the gap may come from exploration, not the update. Match budgets and report seeds.

practice.name: Deep-ML 518: Cliff Walking Sarsa versus Q-Learning
practice.locator: Implement `cliff_walking_comparison`; the public tests call it with `num_episodes=500`, `alpha=0.5`, `gamma=1.0`, `epsilon=0.1`, `seed=42` and expect `(-37.1, -59.7)`, then with `num_episodes=200` and `seed=0` and expect `(-53.7, -63.1)`

units.stopWhen: Your grid passes the single-transition checks, your multi-seed comparison shows the safer Sarsa path against the optimal Q-learning values, and you can explain the gap without appealing to tuning.

units.title: Terminal versus truncated bootstrapping and reward, action, next-state and discount alignment
outcomes: Implement terminal versus truncated bootstrapping: zero beyond termination, keep \(V(S')\) on truncation.
Align reward, action, next state and discount indices on fixed trajectories.
Detect autoreset and done-flag bugs that store fake transitions.
units.why: One wrong zero at a time limit corrupts every value upstream. Termination and truncation look identical in a done flag but demand opposite bootstraps.

next.note: Store the flags the bootstrap needs.
Reuse the bootstrap rule inside DQN targets.

study.title: Terminated versus truncated step API
study.locator: Env `step` returning separate `terminated` and `truncated` flags with `info`, and `reset` with `seed`, including the version 0.26 done-flag split (Gymnasium 1.4.0; page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Terminal values in the control boxes
study.locator: The Sarsa and Q-learning boxes with \(Q(\text{terminal}, \cdot) = 0\) and episodes ending at terminal states (printed pp. 129 to 132)
study.depth: Read for the terminal convention only; control targets live in earlier units.

study.title: Vector autoreset mode
study.locator: Next-step autoreset: the step that ends an episode returns the true final observation, and the next step returns the reset observation (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Run the installed release to confirm the mode, then never store the autoreset step as a transition.

focus: Termination ends the MDP: the target is \(R_{t+1}\) with no bootstrap. Truncation ends the data: the target keeps \(\gamma V(S')\) with \(S'\) the final observation from the truncating step, never the reset observation from the autoreset step.
Index rule: \(R_{t+1}\) and \(S_{t+1}\) belong to \((S_t, A_t)\). The discount \(\gamma\) multiplies the next state's value, never the reward.

Vector next-step autoreset returns the true final observation with flags set, then ignores the next action and returns the reset observation with zero reward. That autoreset step is not a transition and must not be stored.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write both targets for \(R_{t+1} = 1\), \(V(S_{t+1}) = 7\) and \(\gamma = 0.9\): termination gives \(1\) and truncation gives \(1 + 0.9 \times 7 = 7.3\). Then run `CliffWalking-v1` with `reset(seed=0)` and confirm `step` returns separate `terminated` and `truncated` flags.
traps: Collapsing both flags into one done. A time-limit done with zero bootstrap undervalues every state near the limit.
Bootstrapping from the autoreset observation with the ignored action's reward. The reset step carries reward 0 and no flags; storing it trains on a fake transition.
Off-by-one discount exponents. The first reward after \(S_t\) is undiscounted; \(\gamma\) starts applying at the next state's value.

selfTest.q: Time limit hits with value \(7\) ahead. What is the target?
selfTest.a: Keep bootstrapping: \(R + \gamma \times 7\). The limit is truncation, not termination.

selfTest.q: Goal reached with final reward 1. What is the target?
selfTest.a: Exactly 1. Termination zeroes everything beyond.

selfTest.q: A buffer stores the autoreset step as one transition. Why is it fake?
selfTest.a: Its action was ignored and its observation is a fresh reset. It is not a transition from \(s\).

selfTest.q: Reward indices shift by one in the buffer. Which updates break first?
selfTest.a: All n-step and TD targets: every \(R_{t+k}\) pairs with the wrong state.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: seeded alignment and bootstrap defects with terminal-versus-truncated tests.
units.stopWhen: You write both targets from memory, your buffer test rejects autoreset steps, and a shifted-index defect fails loudly.

fit.note: The Gymnasium step API with the terminal convention and the autoreset mode covers both topics at implement depth, with defect practice in the mini-project.

units.title: Trajectory schemas with environment, policy, seed and version identity
outcomes: Define a trajectory record that binds environment, policy, seed and versions to every transition.
Separate training and evaluation streams with distinct seeds and no shared exploration.
Validate records: reject missing identity fields before any update runs.
units.why: RL results change with seeds and versions. Without identity on each record, no comparison is reproducible and no defect is attributable.

next.note: Carry versioned evaluation into continuing-task measurement.
Reuse seed-stream separation at scale.

study.title: Seeding, spec identity and step fields
study.locator: `reset` with `seed` called once after construction, the `spec` version identity, and the `terminated`, `truncated` and `info` step fields (Gymnasium 1.4.0; page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Shared schema in the control laboratory
study.locator: Core requirements and Architecture constraints: one shared transition and trajectory schema with policy and environment version

focus: Each record carries environment id and version, policy id and version, seed, step index, \((s, a, r, s')\), flags and versions. Analysis joins on identity, never on row order.
Evaluation uses distinct seed streams and no training exploration unless the comparison states it. Shared streams leak training noise into evaluation.
Wrappers must not change rewards or termination silently. If a wrapper alters either, its version changes and old records stop mixing with new ones.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, emit one JSON record for a `CliffWalking-v1` step with environment version, policy id, seed, `terminated`, `truncated` and reward, then show a loader accepting it and rejecting the same record with the seed deleted.
traps: Reseeding every episode identically. The same seed replays the same trajectory; streams need distinct seeds drawn from one master seed.
Storing only the environment id. Library versions change dynamics and autoreset behavior, so the version is part of identity.
Letting evaluation share the training RNG. Exploration settings then leak across the boundary the schema was built to enforce.

selfTest.q: Two runs differ only in library version. Comparable?
selfTest.a: Not directly. Version is part of identity; re-run or analyze separately.

selfTest.q: What breaks if the seed is missing from records?
selfTest.a: Attribution. A strange trajectory cannot be replayed or tied to its stream.

selfTest.q: A wrapper clips rewards but keeps the old version. Acceptable?
selfTest.a: No. Silent reward changes invalidate every comparison; version the wrapper and segregate records.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the shared trajectory schema with versioned environment and policy identity.
units.stopWhen: Your loader round-trips a versioned record, rejects identity gaps, and your evaluation streams run on seeds the trainer never used.

fit.note: Gymnasium seeding and spec identity with the laboratory schema contract covers the topic at implement depth, with schema practice in the mini-project.

units.title: Average-reward formulation for continuing tasks
outcomes: Define average reward \(r(\pi)\) and differential returns for continuing tasks.
Derive differential TD errors and state why values hold only up to an additive offset.
Compute the average reward of the three-state ring and explain its differential differences.
units.why: In a continuing task with function approximation, discounting stops being a well-defined objective: averaged over the on-policy distribution it ranks policies exactly as average reward does, and discounted methods lose the policy improvement guarantee. Average reward names the steady rate a never-ending controller earns.

next.note: Carry the continuing-task objective into policy gradients.

study.title: Average reward and differential values
study.locator: Chapter 10, Sections 10.3 to 10.5, equations (10.6), (10.7) and (10.9) to (10.11) with Exercises 10.6 and 10.7 (printed pp. 249 to 255)
study.depth: Read the average-reward definition, differential returns and Exercise 10.7 closely; skim the access-control example and the discounting discussion as context.

focus: Average reward \(r(\pi)\) is the mean reward per step under \(\pi\) from (10.6) and (10.7). Policies order by \(r(\pi)\), and all maximal policies count as optimal.
Differential returns subtract \(r(\pi)\) per step: \(G_t = (R_{t+1} - r(\pi)) + (R_{t+2} - r(\pi)) + \cdots\). Differential Bellman equations drop \(\gamma\) and center rewards.
Adding one constant to every differential value leaves the equations and TD errors unchanged, so algorithms converge up to an offset.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, take the deterministic ring \(A \to B \to C \to A\) with reward \(1\) on arrival in \(A\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Show the average reward is \(1/3\), then show the differential differences satisfy \(v(C) - v(B) = 1/3\) and \(v(B) - v(A) = 1/3\) up to a shared offset.
traps: Treating \(\gamma\) as part of the continuing control problem. Averaged over the on-policy distribution, discounted value equals \(r(\pi)/(1-\gamma)\), so \(\gamma\) cannot change the ranking, and discounted algorithms with function approximation do not optimize that average (Section 10.4).
Pinning absolute differential values. Only differences are identified; demand the offset-free comparison.
Using the raw differential sum on periodic tasks. The plain infinite sum need not converge; Exercise 10.6 motivates the repaired definition (10.13).

selfTest.q: What does Section 10.4 show about discounting in continuing tasks?
selfTest.a: Averaged over the on-policy distribution, discounted value is \(r(\pi)/(1-\gamma)\), so every \(\gamma\) ranks policies like average reward. With function approximation the policy improvement theorem is lost, so discounted algorithms carry no guarantee of optimizing that average.

selfTest.q: What is \(r(\pi)\) for the ring with one reward of 1 per three steps?
selfTest.a: \(1/3\) per step.

selfTest.q: Differential values come out spaced by \(1/3\) up to an offset. Which part matters?
selfTest.a: Pairwise gaps of \(1/3\). Shifting every value by one constant changes nothing in the equations.

selfTest.q: The differential Sarsa box updates the average reward with \(\delta_t\). Why not with the raw reward gap alone?
selfTest.a: With the differential values right, \(\delta_t\) is 0 at every step on the Exercise 10.7 ring, while \(R_{t+1} - \bar{R}\) keeps cycling through 2/3, -1/3 and -1/3. The \(\delta_t\) error gives the steadier average-reward estimate (Exercise 10.8).

practice.name: Sutton and Barto Exercise 10.7: three-state ring average reward
practice.locator: Exercise 10.7: compute the average reward and the differential values of the ring under (10.13)
practice.note: Check the 1/3 rate and the 1/3 gaps against your own derivation. The absolute level is free; the gaps are not.

units.stopWhen: You define \(r(\pi)\) and the differential TD errors without notes and reproduce the ring's \(1/3\) rate with its value gaps.
